facts.label: legend
facts.quote: hoist the flag of Jagannatha which is called as the Patita – Pavana – Bana.
facts.text: The sacred banner hoisted daily atop the temple's crowning wheel is called the Patitapabana Bana, which translates to the purifier of the fallen.

facts.label: legend
facts.quote: Carved on the outer ring are the figures of eight Nava-kunjaras, which is a unique motif in Orissa ikats.
facts.text: The sacred wheel at the apex of the spire, known as the Nila Chakra, is forged from an eight-metal alloy and features eight carved figures of the mythical composite beast Navagunjara on its outer ring.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: This architectural marvel has been declared as a monument of national importance under the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act, 1958 by the Government of India Notification No.2/34/ 72-M dated 3.2.1975
facts.text: The Government of India declared the 12th-century Jagannath Temple in Puri a monument of national importance under the Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act in 1975.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: In 1974, the Archaeological Survey of India (ASI) began the decades-long process of de-plastering the structure. As workers chipped away the white exterior, they revealed intricate bas-reliefs and previously unrecorded epigraphs
facts.text: The Archaeological Survey of India began removing protective lime plaster from the main temple spire in 1974, uncovering intricate 12th-century stone carvings and historic epigraphs beneath.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: The temple was built by the Ganga dynasty king Anantavarman Chodaganga in the 12th century CE, as suggested by the Kendupatna copper-plate inscription of his descendant Narasimhadeva II.
facts.source_name: Epigraphia Indica, Archaeological Survey of India
facts.text: The Kendupatna copper-plate inscription issued by King Narasimhadeva II documents the historical construction of the Purushottama temple by Eastern Ganga ruler King Anantavarman Chodaganga Deva.

facts.label: archaeology
facts.quote: Good quality khondalite stone block was procured from Tapang of undivided Puri district and after proper dressing and carving as per the original design, the new piece was brought inside the temple Bedha and lifted to a height of about 180 feet by heavy lift, iron ropes and jacks and placed in the original position on 28.2.1991.
facts.text: During conservation operations in 1991, the Archaeological Survey of India lifted a replacement khondalite stone to a height of 54.8 metres to repair damaged masonry on the main deula.

facts.label: disputed
facts.quote: According to a story in the temple chronicles, it was founded by Anangabhima-deva II: different chronicles variously mention the year of construction as 1196, 1197, 1205, 1216, or 1226. This suggests that the temple's construction was completed or that the temple was renovated during the reign of Anantavarman's son Anangabhima.
facts.text: Scholars debate whether the existing temple was commissioned and finished by King Anantavarman Chodaganga Deva as indicated by royal epigraphs, or completed by King Anangabhima Deva as claimed in the temple chronicle Madala Panji.

facts.label: disputed
facts.quote: The temple (214 ft. 8 inches high from the road level) is a fine specimen of the 'Pancharatha' style of Odishan temple architecture.
facts.text: The physical height of the main temple shikhara is disputed between traditional and administrative records citing 65.4 metres from street level and trigonometric measurements from the inner courtyard recording 58.5 metres.

facts.label: scripture
facts.quote: The Skanda Purana's Utkal Khanda has a dedicated section to Puri called the 'Purushottama Kshetra Mahatmya', while the Narada Purana and Matsya Purana also refer to Purusottama Kshetra as a sacred location dedicated to Vishnu.
facts.text: The Purushottama Kshetra Mahatmya in the Utkala Khanda of the Skanda Purana details the sacred topography of Nilachala and the religious merit of witnessing the temple's summit.
